sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; exam license with a loophole)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; exam license with a loophole
sections.markdown:
Minnesota runs a **real exam-based license, but it has a gap a chimney fits through.** The **Dept. of Labor & Industry (DLI)** licenses **residential building contractors** and **residential remodelers**, defined as anyone who contracts with an owner to build or improve 1–4 family residential real estate **"by providing two or more special skills"** (Minn. Stat. § 326B.802; licensing duty § 326B.805 subd. 1). The license names a **qualifying person (QP)**, who must pass the state exam and take **14 hours of continuing education every two years** (DLI). *(DLI's license page does not publish the exam's question count or passing score, so we don't cite them.)* **The catch:** § 326B.805 subd. 6 exempts **"specialty contractors who provide only one special skill."** DLI puts it plainly: one-skill specialty contractors "are not required to have a state license (except residential roofers)." A second exemption covers anyone whose gross annual receipts from this work stay **at or under $15,000**. That person must file an affidavit for a **Certificate of Exemption** and renew it every year.

**Where the boundary falls for chimney work (STATE LAW, from the statute's own lists).** § 326B.802 names eight special skills. Two of them name hearth work: **"Masonry and concrete"** includes **"masonry fireplaces"**, and **"General installation specialties"** includes **"fireplaces and wood stoves."** Here is how that sorts out:
- A **masonry-only** chimney or fireplace mason offers one skill and needs **no state license**.
- A shop that does masonry fireplace or chimney work **and also** installs fireplaces, inserts or wood stoves offers **two skills** and **needs the license**.
- Chimney **roof work**, such as re-flashing into the roof covering, can be "residential roofing." Roofers need a **residential roofer license** whatever their skill count (§ 326B.805 subd. 1; DLI).
- **Sweeping or cleaning alone** is not in any of the eight special-skill lists, and DLI's page doesn't mention cleaning or maintenance. On the statute's plain text, a sweep-only business falls outside the license. *(This is our reading of the statute's lists, not a DLI ruling.)*

Bonding is replaced by the **Contractor Recovery Fund** (§ 326B.89). Lookup: **dli.mn.gov** license search.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: The exam tests building code and business, **nothing chimney-specific**. The one-skill and $15,000 exemptions mean many chimney contractors hold **no state credential at all.** Individual certifications (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal.

sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.markdown: **Minn. Stat. §§ 513.52–.60** impose a **narrative "material facts" duty**, not a fixed checklist. Under § 513.55 subd. 1, **"before signing an agreement to sell or transfer residential real property,"** the seller must disclose all material facts they are aware of that could **"adversely and significantly affect"** the buyer's use or enjoyment. The disclosure is made in good faith, to the best of the seller's knowledge. A known cracked flue or unsafe chimney qualifies. The statute itself names no chimney item. *(Industry disclosure forms may itemize fireplace or chimney; we have not verified the current form's wording, so we don't cite it.)* **The disclosure can be waived if seller and buyer agree in writing (§ 513.60).** That waiver does not waive disclosure duties created by other laws. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD.

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown:
Minnesota's remedies come in layers:
- **Home Solicitation Sales (Minn. Stat. §§ 325G.06–.09).** These cover personally solicited sales of goods, services or **improvements to real property over $25** (definition, § 325G.06). The buyer has a **right to cancel until midnight of the third business day** after the sale (§ 325G.07). **Caveat, with a twist that matters for chimneys:** § 325G.06 subd. 2(3) excludes a visit the buyer initiated and "specifically requested ... for the purpose of repairing or performing maintenance," so a sweep the homeowner called in is not itself a solicited sale. But the same clause continues: "If in the course of such a visit, the seller sells the buyer the right to receive additional services or goods other than replacement parts necessarily used in performing the maintenance or in making the repairs, the sale of those additional goods or services would not fall within this exclusion." **So the classic on-site upsell — the sweep who arrives for a cleaning and sells a new liner, crown rebuild or cap — is back inside the home-solicitation rules, and on its face carries the 3-day cancel** (our reading of the statute text; not an AG or court ruling). The door-knock pitch is covered too.
- **Consumer fraud statutes.** The **Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act (§ 325F.69)** and the Deceptive Trade Practices Act can be enforced privately through the AG private-remedy statute (§ 8.31), with attorney's fees.
- **Contractor Recovery Fund (§ 326B.89).** It covers losses from contractors **licensed** as residential contractors or remodelers. Limits are **$100,000 per owner or lessee per licensee**, and **$550,000 total per licensee** (subd. 5, as amended 2024 c 127 art 6 s 2). The older $75k/$150k figures are stale.

These interlock with §1: the fund only pays on *licensed* contractors, so the one-skill exemption that un-licenses chimney-only shops also shuts their customers out of the fund. Complaints go to DLI and the AG.

sections.rawHeading: 5 · Permits & codes (GOV — high confidence; corrected Sep 2026)
sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown:
The **Minnesota State Building Code "is the standard that applies statewide"** (Minn. Stat. § 326B.121). **Enforcement is not universal**, though. A municipality that had adopted the code as of Jan 1, 2008 must keep enforcing it, except municipalities under 2,500 people outside a metropolitan county. Every other municipality **may** adopt it by ordinance. DLI: the code "isn't enforceable by municipalities unless it is adopted by local ordinance." Small rural townships can therefore have little or no permit enforcement (LOCAL).

**Current residential code:** the **2018 IRC**, incorporated by Minn. R. 1309.0010 (published Mar 31, 2020). DLI has started rulemaking toward the **2024** International codes (Request for Comments, Jan 21, 2025, for ch. 1305), but the docket lists **no adoption or effective date yet**. Where the code is enforced, chimney relines, rebuilds and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally permit work; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not.

sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **Minn. Stat. § 299F.51** requires an operational CO alarm **"within ten feet of each room lawfully used for sleeping purposes"** in every single-family dwelling and every multifamily unit, with hotel and lodging rooms also covered. Coverage is broad and standing. There is **no statewide pre-sale certificate.** A permitted chimney job is the natural moment to verify alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban regime; outdoor wood boilers are regulated locally. **Northern Minnesota has among the highest wood-heat density in the country**, making it a core market. *(Market characterization, REF.)*

sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The MN AG publishes standing home-improvement and door-to-door sales guidance. On Oct 14, 2025, the AG sued two remodeling contractors (High Road Builders LLC; Affordable Home Remodeling LLC) under the Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act and Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Those were remodeling prepayment cases, **not chimney work** (ag.state.mn.us/Office/Communications/2025/10/14_Contractors.asp). **No MN chimney-sweep-specific enforcement action has been confirmed.** The AG's release names the Prevention of Consumer Fraud Act, the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the False Statements in Advertisement Act. A door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook § 325G.06 solicited sale. A sweep the buyer requested is not, **but any extra work sold during that visit (beyond necessary replacement parts) falls back under the home-solicitation rules** (§ 325G.06 subd. 2(3)).

sections.title: Season calendar
sections.markdown: Cold statewide and severe in the north. Burn season runs ~Oct–Apr, longer up north. Rush: SEP–NOV. Best booking: APR–JUN.

sections.title: Price seeding (internal)
sections.markdown: The Twin Cities metro runs near or slightly above national prices; greater Minnesota runs below. Use national ranges until listings data exists.

story.heading: The story
story.markdown:
Minnesota looks like a strong-license state, with a genuine exam and a Contractor Recovery Fund; for comparison, Maryland and Virginia run similar regimes. But two escape hatches undercut it exactly where chimneys live.
- **The license only reaches contractors offering two or more special skills.** A masonry-only chimney mason can operate **fully unlicensed and legally**, and a sweep-only business isn't on the statute's skill list at all. The moment a shop both rebuilds masonry fireplaces *and* installs stoves or inserts, it needs the license.
- **The seller's material-facts disclosure can be waived in writing.**

So the credential you'd look up may not exist for your chimney contractor, and the disclosure you'd rely on may have been waived. That is why certification and independent audits matter. And it's one of the highest wood-heat markets in the country.

faq.q: What should I check before hiring a chimney company in Minnesota?
faq.a: State licensing: YES — Residential Building Contractor/Remodeler license (exam) for 2+ special skills; one-skill specialty contractors EXEMPT (§ 326B.805 subd. 6), as are those at or under $15k/yr receipts with a certificate; roofers always licensed. Registration or credential: license + Contractor Recovery Fund ($100k per owner per licensee, $550k aggregate — § 326B.89, 2024 c 127). Seller disclosure at sale: YES — material-facts duty (§ 513.55), WAIVABLE (§ 513.60); statute names no chimney item. Right to cancel a sale made at your home: YES (§ 325G.07; buyer-requested maintenance visit excluded, but add-on goods/services sold during that visit are covered — § 325G.06 subd. 2(3)). Carbon monoxide alarm law: broad (§ 299F.51, within 10 ft of sleeping rooms). Where to check a contractor: dli.mn.gov. Then ask the eight questions below, get the inspection findings in writing with photos, and never sign for "emergency" work on the day of a door-knock.
